description:
Datum Zero is hiring! We are a new team tackling the Burning Activity Calendar challenge: harmonizing 20 years of NASA MODIS & VIIRS fire data into a consistent, easy-to-use view for responders and scientists.

Why join us:

Beginner-friendly: Learn by building a real-world NASA data project with clear tasks.

Hands-on experience: Get practical skills and network with passionate people.

No prior hackathon experience is needed, just curiosity and commitment. Let’s build it together!
summary:
Datum Zero is a web-based fire activity analysis and visualization platform for Southeast Asia. It transforms NASA FIRMS satellite active-fire observations from MODIS and VIIRS into a harmonized monthly calendar, helping users explore how fire activity changes across countries and over time.

The platform provides historical year-by-month heatmaps, country-level analysis, an interactive hotspot map, comparisons with historical baselines, and downloadable data. By accounting for differences between satellite sensors and their observation periods, the project aims to make long-term fire activity patterns easier to interpret and compare.

This matters because understanding when and where fire activity increases can support environmental monitoring, research, land management, and informed preparedness. Datum Zero makes complex satellite observations more accessible through an interactive and intuitive interface. It is an analytical and educational tool, not a substitute for official emergency alerts or ground-based verification.
details:
What the Project Does

Datum Zero — Hotspot Tracker is an interactive web platform that analyzes historical satellite-detected fire activity across Southeast Asia, focusing on Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos. It brings together active-fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments and organizes them into a monthly analytical calendar.

How It Works

The project processes satellite fire observations, standardizes relevant records across different sensors and observation periods, and aggregates the results into a consistent monthly activity metric. The platform presents the processed data through:

  • Fire Activity Calendar: A year-by-month heatmap for exploring seasonal and historical patterns.
  • Country-level Analysis: Users can select a country and examine its fire activity over time.
  • Interactive Hotspot Map: A geographic view of aggregated fire activity, with selectable areas and spatial exploration.
  • Historical Comparison: Users can compare selected periods against historical baselines to identify unusually high or low activity.
  • Data Export: Users can download analytical results in CSV format for further investigation.

Benefits and Intended Impact

By turning complex satellite observations into accessible visual information, Datum Zero helps students, researchers, environmental analysts, and land managers identify recurring fire seasons, examine changes over time, and investigate areas of interest. The platform is designed to support environmental awareness, research, and informed preparedness.

Technology and Tools

  • Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m active-fire products, including Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI for data processing and API services.
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • Mapping: Leaflet and CARTO basemaps.
  • Geospatial preparation: QGIS and Natural Earth geographic datasets.
  • Interface libraries: Tailwind CSS and Lucide icons.
  • Deployment: Render.

Creativity and Considerations

The project's key contribution is its sensor-aware approach to presenting long-term fire activity. Raw hotspot detections from different satellite instruments should not automatically be treated as directly comparable because their spatial resolutions, observation periods, and sensor characteristics differ. Datum Zero aims to make these differences more understandable through harmonized analysis and clear visual explanations.

The platform displays satellite-detected active-fire observations, not confirmed fire perimeters or burned area. Aggregated map cells represent summarized activity rather than individual fire incidents. Historical comparisons indicate deviations from a baseline; they should not be interpreted as machine-learning predictions or official emergency warnings.
